strengths: Christopoulos clearly framed the dispute through priors and comparative likelihoods, directly connecting evidential strength to the probability required by the motion.
His likelihood-ratio formulation kept the affirmative case comparative rather than treating resurrection as established merely because some supporting reports exist.
He assembled a cumulative historical case from source indicators, known burial, an empty tomb, reported appearances, conversion, and costly witness conduct.
His incarnation argument was appropriately conditional and modest, claiming only that contested theistic background assumptions could prevent a prohibitively low prior.

blunders.text: The stable-natural-order argument established compatibility between regularity and miracles, but it did not adequately answer why pervasive mortality should not still lower resurrection's prior probability.
The source and empty-tomb cases bundled several disputed considerations without sufficiently establishing document-specific independence, confirmed witnesses, or the necessary burial sequence.
Appeals to sincerity, persecution, and willingness to die supported committed belief more readily than the truth or accurate transmission of the underlying resurrection claim.

strengths: Dillahunty sharply distinguished the probability of receiving resurrection reports if resurrection occurred from the probability that resurrection occurred given those reports.
He repeatedly separated sincerity and costly commitment from truth, directly answering the affirmative reliance on transformed and suffering witnesses.
He identified death, burial, and prior occupancy of a tomb as necessary evidential foundations that require support before an empty tomb can carry explanatory weight.
He preserved rational uncertainty as a legitimate conclusion when neither resurrection nor any particular natural alternative receives sufficiently grounded probability assignments.
His alternatives argument correctly maintained that weaknesses in individual natural explanations do not themselves supply affirmative evidence for resurrection.

blunders.text: The demand for empirical evidence, confirmed primary witnesses, contemporary corroboration, and independent investigation was forceful but sometimes stated too categorically for an ancient historical inquiry.

The divine-action critique challenged incarnation and sacrificial suffering, but it did less to address the affirmative's narrower conditional claim that theistic background beliefs could alter the prior.
The account-disparity objection identified a real reliability issue, yet it did not specify which differences were irreconcilable or how strongly each one should reduce the cumulative case.

newArguments.title: Robustness Across Source Models
newArguments.text: Instead of asking whether the New Testament is globally reliable, construct several source models ranging from substantial dependence and later transmission to greater independence and proximity. Estimate the resurrection comparison within each model. If the same limited core of facts favors resurrection even under skeptical but plausible dependence assumptions, the inference gains robustness without pretending that every narrative detail is secure. If the result disappears whenever independence is reduced, the affirmative should concede that its case depends on a fragile source reconstruction.

novelty.explanation: This introduces a model-robustness test not stated in the locked affirmative moves and therefore has no transcript source move.

newArguments.title: Prediction-Specific Rival Comparison
newArguments.text: Natural rivals should be divided by what they predict rather than dismissed one at a time. A bereavement-experience model may predict sincere appearances but not an empty known tomb; fabrication may predict coordinated proclamation but less readily costly persistence by initial claimants; mistaken burial may predict absence but not diverse encounters. Resurrection earns comparative force only if one supported evidence set strains these rivals simultaneously, with overlap and dependence discounted. This approach turns the cumulative case into explicit discriminating predictions instead of an appeal to unexplained residue.

novelty.explanation: This is a new prediction-partition method for comparing composite rivals rather than a restatement of the live likelihood-ratio claim.

newArguments.title: Dependence Penalty for Evidence Bundles
newArguments.text: The affirmative evidence should not be multiplied as though burial reports, empty-tomb narratives, appearances, and later witness traditions were independent observations. Shared communities, texts, theological expectations, and repeated retelling can generate several reported features from fewer underlying information channels. A formal dependence penalty would lower the cumulative force whenever claims travel together. The skeptical point is not that dependence proves falsehood, but that an apparently large evidence bundle may contain far less independent information than its item count suggests.

novelty.explanation: This introduces an explicit dependence penalty for cumulative evidence, a method absent from the locked skeptical moves.

newArguments.title: Imprecise Probability and Suspension
newArguments.text: Where numerical priors and likelihoods cannot be responsibly fixed, represent them as ranges rather than invented point values. If plausible ranges for source reliability, death confirmation, tomb occupancy, visionary experiences, and transmission overlap enough that different reasonable settings yield different leading hypotheses, no stable ranking follows. Suspension is then supported by model instability, not merely by missing information or personal incredulity. This also supplies a principled stopping rule: belief becomes warranted only when the same conclusion persists across the defensible parameter region.

novelty.explanation: This adds an imprecise-probability framework and robustness criterion not articulated in the transcript inventory.
